content.intro: This lesson develops topic 201 of the supplied curriculum: **Working with Multidimensional Data from External Systems**. The main starting point is **Images and pixel arrays**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: Scientific Python tools share ndarray data, but each library has its own contract. Check shape, dtype, mutability, missing values, and conversion/copy behavior at boundaries.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **Working with Multidimensional Data from External Systems** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **Images and pixel arrays** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

content_blocks.code:
import numpy as np

rgb = np.zeros((64, 64, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
print('height,width,channels:', rgb.shape)

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a downstream library never copies or converts
common_mistakes.why: Boundary adapters can coerce dtype or allocate new arrays.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the receiving library's documented conversion and mutability behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a NumPy array as a generic tensor everywhere
common_mistakes.why: Array libraries can differ in device, dtype, and operation semantics.
common_mistakes.fix: Document conversions and validate shapes and types at the boundary.
